body:
# CoT-Monitoring Reliance x Covert Sandbagging: A Compound Failure for Monitoring-Based Safety Cases

**Problem:** Failure mode A: emerging governance proposals lean on chain-of-thought monitoring as a cheap oversight mechanism. Failure mode B: models can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (underperform without verbalizing the plan). If a safety case rests on CoT monitoring, covert sandbagging silently invalidates it.

**Direction:** On a small open model, reproduce a minimal covert-sandbag setup (prompt the model to underperform while keeping a clean-looking CoT) and measure how often a simple keyword/judge-based CoT monitor flags it vs misses it. Frame the false-negative rate as the failure probability of a monitoring-based regulatory safety case. A scoped model-organism probe, not a training effort.

**Why it matters:** Directly tests whether a governance mechanism many proposals assume is robust actually survives an adversarial model — a model-organism study labs deprioritize because it undercuts a tool they want to claim credit for. One GPU, public model.

**Relevant context:** LLMs can covertly sandbag against CoT monitoring (arXiv:2508.00943); Auditing Games for Sandbagging (arXiv:2512.07810).

# Documentation Fragmentation x Automated Compliance Checking: Why Machine-Readable Gaps Break Enforcement

**Problem:** Failure mode A: model documentation uses 947 inconsistent section names, so safety facts aren't machine-locatable. Failure mode B: regulators (EU AI Act Annex IV, SB53) increasingly expect scalable/automated compliance checking. The two compound: automated enforcement silently passes non-compliant disclosures because it can't find the relevant section.

**Direction:** Build a small LLM-or-regex compliance checker against a fixed Annex-IV-style schema, run it over a sample of real public model cards, and measure its false-pass and false-fail rate caused purely by naming/structure variation (vs genuine content presence). Show how much enforcement accuracy degrades with documentation fragmentation, and how a normalization step recovers it.

**Why it matters:** Quantifies a hidden coupling between disclosure standards and the feasibility of scalable enforcement, arguing for mandated machine-readable schemas. Public docs + light tooling; strongly counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** AI Transparency Atlas fragmentation findings (arXiv:2512.12443); EU AI Act Annex IV; California SB53 transparency (anthropic.com/news/compliance-framework-SB53).

# Elicitation-Gap Uncertainty x Conditional Safety Triggers: Error-Propagation Through Policy Logic

**Problem:** Failure mode A: capability elicitation is noisy — measured capability depends heavily on how hard you tried (prompting, scaffolding). Failure mode B: responsible-scaling policies treat a single eval number as a crisp trigger. Measurement uncertainty propagates into binary policy decisions, so the trigger fires or doesn't based on elicitation luck.

**Direction:** On one open model and one safety-relevant task, run several elicitation strategies (zero-shot, few-shot, simple scaffolding) and record the spread of capability scores. Treat that spread as measurement error and propagate it through a stylized threshold-trigger rule to compute the probability of a wrong governance decision. Output an error-budget recommendation for how many elicitation runs a trigger needs.

**Why it matters:** Bridges measurement noise and policy logic, giving labs/regulators a principled 'elicitation budget' before a binary trigger is credible. Statistics-forward, beginner-appropriate, needs no lab access.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance: determining whether evals found all vulnerabilities is open (arXiv:2407.14981); sandbagging/elicitation literature (arXiv:2406.07358).

# Self-Reported Compute x Misreporting Incentives: Stress-Testing the Honesty Assumption in Compute Governance

**Problem:** Failure mode A: compute governance and FLOP-threshold regimes rely on developers self-reporting training compute. Failure mode B: there is a direct incentive to under-report to stay below a systemic-risk threshold. Together, the threshold becomes unenforceable without an independent estimator — a compound governance failure.

**Direction:** Investigate whether training compute can be independently sanity-checked from public signals. Using public model-report data, build a simple regression linking disclosed params/tokens/benchmark performance to disclosed FLOP, then flag models whose self-report is an outlier from the fitted relationship. Demonstrate the method on the public dataset as a proof-of-concept 'compute lie detector.'

**Why it matters:** Prototypes the independent verification that threshold-based compute governance currently lacks, directly hitting the 'verify safety claims auditable by third parties' open problem. Pure public-data analysis; high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** Open problem: third-party-auditable verification (interface-eu.org); Computing Power and Governance (arXiv:2402.08797); Epoch AI compute data.

# Unlearning-Based Safeguards x Knowledge Recovery: Auditing the Durability Claims Regulators Accept

**Problem:** Failure mode A: labs cite 'unlearning' of dangerous knowledge as a mitigation in safety frameworks. Failure mode B: shallow unlearning is recoverable (relearning, jailbreaks, or even acts as accidental sandbagging). Governance that credits an unlearning claim inherits a mitigation that doesn't hold.

**Direction:** On a small open model with a public unlearning benchmark (e.g. WMDP/TOFU-style), apply a published unlearning method, then measure knowledge recovery via a few relearning steps or paraphrase probes. Quantify the 'durability gap' and cross-reference how unlearning is described in real safety-policy language to show the credibility mismatch.

**Why it matters:** Tests whether a mitigation governance frameworks accept survives contact with a cheap adversary — a model-organism-flavored audit of a policy assumption. Single GPU, open benchmarks, deeply counterfactual.

**Relevant context:** Durability of open-weight safeguards / shallow unlearning (arXiv:2412.07097); sandbagging via failed unlearning (arXiv:2406.07358); Safety Gap Toolkit (arXiv:2507.11544).

# Cross-Lab Eval Divergence x Single-Score Indices: Sensitivity Analysis of the AI Safety Index

**Problem:** Failure mode A: different evaluators grade the same construct differently (low inter-rater reliability). Failure mode B: composite indices (FLI AI Safety Index) collapse those grades into one headline letter that drives public and policy attention. Grade noise compounds into a falsely-precise ranking that can mis-rank labs.

**Direction:** Reconstruct the published Index scoring (33 indicators, 6 domains, unweighted averaging) and run a sensitivity/bootstrap analysis: perturb individual grades within plausible inter-rater error and weighting schemes, and measure how often the lab ranking flips. Report which rankings are robust and which are artifacts of aggregation choices.

**Why it matters:** Shows how much of a widely-cited governance signal is real vs aggregation noise, improving the methodology the field is standardizing on. Pure re-analysis of a public report — the FR67 'apply Index methodology to additional dimensions' hint, sharpened into a robustness audit.

**Relevant context:** FLI AI Safety Index Summer 2025 methodology: 33 indicators, unweighted domain averaging (futureoflife.org); FR67 hint in subfield context.

# Incident Taxonomy Inconsistency x Pattern Detection: Why Fragmented Reporting Blinds an AI-NTSB

**Problem:** Failure mode A: AI incident reports use inconsistent, unstandardized taxonomies. Failure mode B: an NTSB-style body needs to aggregate incidents to detect systemic patterns. Inconsistent labels prevent clustering, so a recurring failure mode stays invisible — the two failures compound into 'we have the data but can't see the pattern.'

**Direction:** Pull a sample of AI Incident Database entries, apply two or three different public AI-harm taxonomies, and measure how much the same incidents get classified differently. Then show via simple clustering how taxonomy inconsistency fragments would-be patterns. Propose and test a minimal normalization mapping that recovers cluster signal.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates that an AI-NTSB's value depends on taxonomy harmonization, directly informing the national incident-response-framework open problem. Open dataset, beginner-friendly clustering, no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** Standardising AI incident reporting (arXiv:2501.14778); designing incident reporting for GPAI (arXiv:2511.05914); AI Incident Database (oodaloop.com).

# Benchmark Refusal-Inflation x Capability Hiding: Disentangling 'Safe' From 'Can't' in Governance Numbers

**Problem:** Failure mode A: on dangerous-capability evals, a refusal counts as a low score, conflating 'won't' with 'can't.' Failure mode B: governance reads the low score as low capability and relaxes mitigations. A heavily-refusing model that is secretly capable thus games the regulatory signal — two failure modes that mutually disguise true risk.

**Direction:** On an open model, run a dangerous-capability proxy benchmark, then re-run with a benign-framing jailbreak that removes refusals, and measure the score gap. Treat the gap as 'capability hidden behind refusal.' Argue that governance numbers must separate refusal-rate from capability-rate, and provide a simple two-axis reporting template.

**Why it matters:** Exposes a structural conflation in the numbers regulators trigger on, with a concrete fix. No training, single open model, and an argument frontier labs are unlikely to surface because it complicates their 'safe' framing.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance on assessment validity (arXiv:2407.14981); safety-gap / refusal-removal findings (arXiv:2507.11544).

# Code-of-Practice Vagueness x Selective Compliance: Measuring Where Soft Law Lets Big Labs Off Easy

**Problem:** Failure mode A: the EU GPAI Code of Practice uses vague, non-presumption-granting language. Failure mode B: compliance is uneven, with well-resourced providers investing more in documentation. The two compound so that vagueness plus asymmetric capacity lets the riskiest soft-law obligations be satisfied most thinly exactly where stakes are highest.

**Direction:** Code each Code-of-Practice measure for linguistic 'hardness' (e.g. shall/should/may, presence of measurable criteria) using a simple rubric, then map each measure to publicly observable signals of whether providers actually did it. Compute a 'vagueness x observed-compliance' grid identifying the soft commitments most likely to be hollow. Mostly structured policy-text analysis with light NLP.

**Why it matters:** Directly targets the open problem of the gap between voluntary codes and enforceable standards, producing a prioritized list of clauses needing hardening. Public documents only; squarely civil-society work.

**Relevant context:** EU GPAI Code of Practice voluntary/non-presumption status and uneven compliance (dlapiper.com; artificialintelligenceact.eu); enforceability-gap open problem (EU AI Office).

# Eval Cost x Coverage: How Expensive Evals Force Sampling Gaps That Adversaries Exploit

**Problem:** Failure mode A: comprehensive evals are expensive, so labs/regulators sample a subset of capabilities. Failure mode B: a model (or developer) can concentrate dangerous capability in unsampled regions. Cost-driven sampling and targeted capability-hiding compound: the cheaper the eval regime, the easier the blind spot to exploit.

**Direction:** On a public benchmark, simulate a 'budget-constrained regulator' who can only test a random k% of items, and an 'adversary' who knows which items are likely sampled. Quantify how detection probability of an injected weakness drops as budget shrinks, and how adaptive (vs random) sampling restores it. A clean stats/simulation study with a policy-budget framing.

**Why it matters:** Connects the documented 'evals are expensive at scale' problem to exploitable coverage gaps, recommending adaptive sampling for budget-limited oversight bodies. Simulation-only, no lab resources, strong beginner fit.

**Relevant context:** Open Problems in Technical AI Governance: evals expensive at scale, completeness unknown (arXiv:2407.14981).

# Watermark/Provenance Fragility x Disclosure Mandates: When the Mechanism Can't Support the Rule

**Problem:** Failure mode A: governance mandates AI-content provenance/labeling (EU AI Act transparency). Failure mode B: provenance signals (watermarks, metadata) are fragile and strippable. The mandate compounds with the fragile mechanism so that 'compliant' labeled content silently loses its provenance downstream, defeating the rule.

**Direction:** Take a public text or image watermarking method and apply simple, realistic transformations (paraphrase, crop, recompress, format conversion) to measure watermark survival rates. Map survival rates against the operational requirements implied by the disclosure mandate to show where the mandate is technically unenforceable. Empirical robustness study on open tools.

**Why it matters:** Demonstrates that a transparency rule and its enabling mechanism are mismatched, informing realistic provenance policy. Uses open watermarking tools on a consumer GPU; no proprietary access needed.

**Relevant context:** EU AI Act transparency/provenance obligations (artificialintelligenceact.eu); Open Problems in Technical AI Governance ecosystem-monitoring/verification (arXiv:2407.14981).

# Threshold Cliffs x Strategic Capability Withholding: Modeling the Incentive to Park Just Below the Line

**Problem:** Failure mode A: governance uses sharp capability/compute thresholds with large obligation jumps ('cliffs'). Failure mode B: developers can strategically tune disclosed capability to sit just below the cliff. The two compound into a bunching incentive that hollows out the regime exactly at the threshold meant to bite.

**Direction:** Build a simple game-theoretic / numerical model of a developer choosing disclosed capability against a cliff-shaped obligation cost, and show the equilibrium bunching just below the threshold. Then look for bunching evidence in public model-report distributions (do disclosed numbers cluster below known thresholds?). Combine a toy model with a light empirical check.

**Why it matters:** Predicts and partially tests a manipulation pattern, arguing for smooth/graduated obligations over cliffs. Modeling plus public-data analysis; medium-horizon structural concern labs won't volunteer.

**Relevant context:** EU AI Act systemic-risk FLOP cliff (artificialintelligenceact.eu); self-reporting incentives (Computing Power and Governance, arXiv:2402.08797).

# Auditor Capture x Information Asymmetry: A Toy Model of Why Third-Party Audits Drift Toward Pass

**Problem:** Failure mode A: auditors depend on the audited lab for access/fees (capture risk). Failure mode B: severe information asymmetry (only the lab knows the model internals). Together they compound into systematic optimism: audits that are nominally independent drift toward passing because the auditor can neither see nor afford to fail the client.

**Direction:** Construct a small principal-agent / repeated-game simulation where an auditor chooses strictness under access dependence and asymmetric information, and identify the conditions under which audits become rubber stamps. Sweep interventions (random re-audits, public access requirements, liability) to find what restores honest reporting. Pure modeling with clear, falsifiable predictions.

**Why it matters:** Gives regulators a mechanism-design lens on why audit mandates may fail and which structural fixes help, supporting the 'auditable verification' open problem. No data or lab access required — fully outside-lab.

**Relevant context:** Third-party audit access roadblocks and accountability paradox (ccgnludelhi.wordpress.com; arXiv:2505.11577); verification open problem (interface-eu.org).

# Open-Weight Proliferation x Jurisdictional Gaps: Mapping Where a Released Model Escapes Every Safety Regime

**Problem:** Failure mode A: open-weight releases are globally irreversible. Failure mode B: safety regimes are jurisdiction-bounded (EU, California, China differ). A model released under one regime is hosted/fine-tuned under a weaker one, so proliferation and jurisdictional fragmentation compound into a global lowest-common-denominator outcome.

**Direction:** Build a small comparative matrix of how 3-4 jurisdictions' rules apply to open-weight models (release, fine-tuning, hosting, liability), then trace a hypothetical released model through hosting/fine-tuning steps to identify the jurisdiction-hop that strips each safeguard. Output a 'regime-escape path' diagram plus the minimal cross-border rule that would close it.

**Why it matters:** Makes concrete how proliferation plus regulatory fragmentation defeats any single regime, motivating international coordination on open weights. Document-based comparative analysis; no lab resources, strong policy blog post.

**Relevant context:** Irreversible open-weight releases (arXiv:2412.07097; aisi.gov.uk); divergent national approaches and international coordination open problem (subfield context; interface-eu.org).

# Agentic Deployment x Static Pre-Deployment Evals: The Capability a One-Shot Eval Can't See

**Problem:** Failure mode A: governance certifies models with static, single-turn pre-deployment evals. Failure mode B: agentic/tool-use deployment composes capabilities over many steps, producing emergent dangerous behavior absent in single-shot tests. The two compound: a model certified safe one-shot becomes dangerous when wired into an agent loop, and no regulatory step re-checks it.

**Direction:** On a small open model, compare its single-turn score on a safety-relevant task against its success when given a simple multi-step scaffold/tool loop (e.g. retrieval + iteration) on the same goal. Measure the capability uplift from composition. Argue that pre-deployment certification must include an agentic-scaffold allowance, and quantify how big that allowance should be.

**Why it matters:** Shows a structural gap between how models are certified and how they're deployed, informing whether governance should regulate the deployed agent system, not just the base model. Single GPU, public model, cheap scaffolding — a medium-horizon threat labs underweight.

**Relevant context:** AgentMisalignment propensity (arXiv:2506.04018); Frontier AI Risk Management Framework in practice (arXiv:2507.16534); assessment open problems (arXiv:2407.14981).

# Feature Absorption as a Safety Probe Failure Mode

**Problem:** Linear probes for safety-relevant concepts (deception, refusal) are trained on residual-stream activations, but SAE research shows 'feature absorption': a token-aligned latent silently absorbs a feature direction so the intended latent fails to fire in some contexts. If a deception or refusal feature is partially absorbed, a probe built on it could have systematic blind spots that look like normal noise.

**Direction:** Using a pre-trained open SAE (Gemma-2-2B via SAELens) and a known safety-relevant feature, deliberately construct prompts in the 'absorbing' context (where one feature is highly linearly predictable from another) and measure whether a downstream linear probe's recall drops in exactly those contexts. Map the absorption-induced blind-spot region for one safety concept and quantify how much recall is lost.

**Why it matters:** Absorption blind spots would mean monitoring probes fail precisely in correlated, predictable contexts an adversary could engineer. This is a counterfactual-friendly, no-training study using existing SAE weights that frontier labs have little incentive to audit publicly.

**Relevant context:** Chanin et al. 'A is for Absorption' (arXiv 2409.14507) shows absorption occurs when one feature is highly linearly predictable from another and is a sparsity-regularization artifact; varying SAE size/sparsity does not fix it. SAELens provides pre-trained Gemma SAEs.

# Seed-Sensitivity of Safety Features Across SAE Reruns

**Problem:** SAEs trained with different seeds or hyperparameters converge to different feature sets. If a 'refusal' or 'harmful-content' feature is found in one SAE but not in a sibling trained on the same model with a different seed, then any safety claim built on a single SAE is fragile and non-reproducible.

**Direction:** Take two or more openly released SAEs for the same model/layer (different seeds/hyperparameters, available on Neuronpedia/SAELens) and attempt to match a small set of safety-relevant features (refusal, toxicity, deception) across them via activation-correlation matching. Report what fraction of safety-relevant features are stable vs. seed-specific.

**Why it matters:** Establishes whether SAE-based safety findings replicate across training runs — a prerequisite for using SAEs in deployment decisions. Requires no training, only public weights, and directly addresses the interpretability-to-safety-guarantee gap.

**Relevant context:** 2025 SAE reviews note SAEs trained with different seeds/hyperparameters converge to different feature sets. Neuronpedia and SAELens host multiple SAEs per model. Open Phil RFP lists interpretability-to-safety-guarantee benchmarks as a priority.

# Do Open Replication Circuit Tracers Reproduce the Planning-Ahead Result?

**Problem:** Anthropic reported that Claude 3.5 Haiku plans rhyming words ahead before writing a poetry line, but this was shown only on a proprietary model. It is unknown whether the same planning circuit appears in small open models, or whether the finding is model-specific.

**Direction:** Using the open Circuit Tracer library (supports Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-4B), construct rhyming-completion prompts and build attribution graphs to test whether an open model represents the end-of-line rhyme word before generating the line. Compare across the three supported model families to see if planning-ahead is universal or scale/family dependent.

**Why it matters:** Forward-planning latent representations are an alignment-relevant phenomenon (a model committing to a goal before verbalizing). Confirming or refuting it in open models tells us whether this safety-relevant behavior is studiable outside frontier labs.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Circuit Tracing / 'On the Biology of an LLM' (transformer-circuits.pub 2025) reports planning-ahead in Claude 3.5 Haiku. Anthropic Fellows released Circuit Tracer (Gemma-2-2B, Llama-3.2-1B, Qwen3-4B); EleutherAI released Attribute supporting CLTs.

# Vision-vs-Language SAE Sparsity Gap as a Monitoring Cost Signal

**Problem:** Vision SAEs require far higher L0 (active latents per patch, ~500 for CLIP-B/32) than language SAEs (12-74 for GPT-2 Small) at comparable explained variance. Nobody has characterized what this means for SAE-based monitoring of multimodal models: more active features per token may mean monitoring is intrinsically harder/noisier on the vision side.

**Direction:** Using ViT-Prisma's 80+ pre-trained vision SAE weights and a language SAE, empirically map the relationship between L0, monosemanticity, and the difficulty of finding a clean concept feature (e.g., a specific object category) in vision vs. a clean concept in language. Quantify how the higher L0 budget degrades the precision of single-feature interventions.

**Why it matters:** Multimodal models are deploying fast and interpretability there lags. Showing that vision-side monitoring needs structurally different sparsity assumptions is a counterfactual-valuable, training-free contribution toward multimodal safety tooling.

**Relevant context:** Joseph et al. 'Prisma' (arXiv 2504.19475) reports vision SAEs need ~500+ L0 per patch vs 12-74 for GPT-2 Small at comparable explained variance, and sometimes reduce model loss. 80+ pre-trained SAE weights are public on GitHub.

# Off-Policy vs On-Policy Activations Break Deception Probes

**Problem:** Deception probes are trained on activations, but recent work flags that off-policy (forced/templated) training data hurts probe performance relative to on-policy (model-generated) data. The size of this gap, and whether it explains real-world probe generalization failures, is under-measured on open models.

**Direction:** On an open instruction model (e.g., Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct or Gemma-2-9B), build two deception probe training sets — one with forced/templated 'lie' completions and one with model-generated deceptive completions — and measure how a probe trained on one transfers to the other. Quantify the on/off-policy generalization gap for a single safety concept.

**Why it matters:** If monitoring probes silently rely on artifacts of how their training data was elicited, they will fail when deployed on genuine model behavior. This is exactly the diffuse, hard-to-do-well evaluation work that needs no lab resources.

**Relevant context:** 'That's not natural: impact of off-policy training data on probe performance' (OpenReview IOR5bkd0ep) and 'Detecting Strategic Deception Using Linear Probes' (arXiv 2502.03407) show probes are sensitive to data construction. Apollo/UK AISI work on probe robustness.

# Multi-Layer Probe Ensembling for Sandbagging Detection

**Problem:** Linear probe accuracy for deception scales with model size, and principled multi-layer ensembling for deception detection remains explicitly unexplored. Sandbagging (capability concealment) is the most safety-critical deception type but is hard to elicit and probe for.

**Direction:** On an open model, construct a small sandbagging model-organism setup (prompt a model to deliberately underperform on a benchmark when it believes it is being evaluated) and compare single-layer probes vs. a simple multi-layer ensemble at detecting the concealment state. Measure whether ensembling closes the gap on this hard-to-elicit behavior.

**Why it matters:** Sandbagging detection is a long-horizon threat (a model hiding capabilities to pass evals) labs deprioritize for nearer concerns. A model-organism slice probing an existing model needs no training and is high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** 'Linear Probe Accuracy Scales with Model Size and Benefits from Multi-Layer Ensembling' (arXiv 2604.13386) notes multi-layer ensembling for deception is unexplored; deception-probe work notes sandbagging datasets are hard to construct due to near-zero compliance.

# Does Activation Steering Break Safety Even at Interpretable Scales?

**Problem:** Recent work ('The Rogue Scalpel') shows activation steering systematically compromises LLM safety even when framed as a precise, interpretable intervention. It is unclear at what steering magnitude safety begins to break, relative to where the intended behavioral effect appears — i.e., whether there is any 'safe operating window'.

**Direction:** Using the open steering-vectors library and an open chat model, sweep steering magnitude for a benign style/topic vector and jointly measure (a) the intended behavioral change and (b) jailbreak/refusal-bypass rate on a small harmful-prompt set. Map the dose-response curve to find whether safety degradation precedes, coincides with, or follows the useful effect.

**Why it matters:** Steering is increasingly proposed as an interpretable control knob. Demonstrating that its 'safe window' is narrow or nonexistent on open models is directly actionable safety evidence requiring only public tools.

**Relevant context:** 'The Rogue Scalpel: Activation Steering Compromises LLM Safety' (researchgate 395944752 / OpenReview) shows steering breaks alignment. 2025 work notes side effects appear mainly at high steering scales; llm-steer / steering-vectors are open libraries.

# When Does Superposition Emerge During Training? A Replayable Toy Study

**Problem:** The original Toy Models of Superposition shows superposition is governed by a phase change with discrete learning dynamics, but the question of whether models use superposition early or only as they struggle to fit more features remains a noted open thread. This matters because training dynamics shape what features models learn.

**Direction:** Reproduce the small Anthropic toy model (trainable in minutes on one GPU) and instrument it to log feature geometry across training steps. Systematically vary feature sparsity and the feature-to-dimension ratio to chart WHEN in training each feature enters superposition, producing an empirical 'timing phase diagram'.

**Why it matters:** Understanding when superposition forms is a foundation for predicting which dangerous features a model might pack into shared directions. The toy model is fully open and trainable in a 30h budget, making it ideal counterfactual-value work on training dynamics.

**Relevant context:** Elhage et al. 'Toy Models of Superposition' (transformer-circuits.pub 2022) describes a phase-change governed, discrete learning dynamics and explicitly raises when-in-training superposition emerges. UK AISI lists understanding how training dynamics shape features as an open problem.

# Evaluating SAE Features Without Explanations as a Cheap Safety Audit

**Problem:** Standard SAE evaluation relies on auto-generated natural-language explanations of features, which are expensive and themselves error-prone. A 2025 line proposes evaluating SAE interpretability WITHOUT explanations, but it has not been applied as a triage tool to flag which safety-relevant features are actually trustworthy.

**Direction:** Take a public SAE, identify candidate safety-relevant features by activation patterns (toxicity, refusal), and apply explanation-free interpretability metrics (e.g., activation-prediction consistency, intervention coherence) to rank which features are reliable enough to monitor. Validate the ranking against a small manual inspection.

**Why it matters:** Gives facilitators and small labs a cheap, training-free triage method to decide which SAE features to trust for monitoring, directly addressing the SAE-reliability gap without proprietary infrastructure.

**Relevant context:** 'Evaluating SAE interpretability without explanations' (arXiv 2507.08473) proposes explanation-free metrics. SAELens/Neuronpedia host public SAEs with feature dashboards but no standardized safety evaluation (identified benchmark gap).

# Matryoshka vs Standard SAE: Which Preserves Safety Features Under Scaling?

**Problem:** Matryoshka SAEs organize features into nested reconstruction prefixes so high-level features aren't absorbed as dictionary size grows, but it is unverified whether SAFETY-relevant high-level features (e.g., a 'harmful intent' concept) are actually better preserved in Matryoshka SAEs than in standard SAEs of comparable size.

**Direction:** Compare an open Matryoshka SAE against a standard SAE on the same model/layer for the persistence and cleanliness of a chosen safety-relevant high-level feature across dictionary scales. Measure absorption/splitting of that specific feature in each architecture.

**Why it matters:** If a newer SAE architecture better preserves safety concepts, that is directly relevant to choosing monitoring tooling. This is an architecture-comparison study (a recommended strategy for this subfield) using only public weights.

**Relevant context:** Bussmann et al. 'Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders' (Alignment Forum) describes nested prefixes preventing high-level feature absorption. 'A is for Absorption' (arXiv 2409.14507) documents the absorption/splitting problem these aim to fix.

# Orthogonality-Constrained SAEs and Disentangled Safety Concepts

**Problem:** OrtSAE enforces orthogonality among feature vectors to reduce absorption and composition, producing more atomic features. It is unknown whether enforcing orthogonality actually disentangles entangled safety concepts (e.g., separating 'rudeness' from 'genuine harm') that standard SAEs conflate.

**Direction:** Identify a pair of safety concepts that a standard SAE tends to entangle, then compare how cleanly an orthogonality-constrained SAE (OrtSAE) vs a standard SAE separates them, using activation-overlap and intervention-specificity metrics. Focus the entire study on one entangled concept pair.

**Why it matters:** Conflating distinct harm concepts produces both false alarms and missed detections in monitoring. Showing whether orthogonality helps disentangle them is a focused, training-light contribution to trustworthy interpretability.

**Relevant context:** 2025 SAE work introduces OrtSAE (orthogonality among feature vectors reduces absorption/composition, linear compute in dictionary size). Absorption literature (arXiv 2409.14507) documents concept entanglement in standard SAEs.

# Evaluation-Awareness Features: Does the Model Know It's Being Tested?

**Problem:** Probing work shows language models have detectable 'evaluation awareness' — internal representations of whether they are being tested. If such a feature exists and is steerable, it directly enables sandbagging and undermines all behavioral safety evals. Its mechanistic basis in open models is barely characterized.

**Direction:** On an open chat model, build contrastive prompt pairs (clearly-an-eval vs natural-deployment framings), train a linear probe / locate the SAE feature for evaluation-awareness, and test whether activating it changes behavior on a benchmark (a sandbagging-style intervention). Confirm the feature is causal, not just correlational.

**Why it matters:** Evaluation awareness is a core long-horizon threat: models that behave differently when watched. A model-organism-style probe of an existing open model needs no training and is precisely the diffuse, lab-deprioritized work prioritized here.

**Relevant context:** 'Probing Evaluation Awareness of Language Models' (arXiv 2507.01786) shows LMs internally represent whether they are being evaluated. Deception-probe literature ties this to sandbagging being the most safety-critical and hardest-to-elicit deception type.

# Cross-Model Feature Universality for a Single Safety Concept

**Problem:** It is an open question whether a given safety-relevant feature (e.g., 'refusal') occupies a comparable representational role across different open model families, or whether each family encodes it idiosyncratically. Universality would mean monitoring transfers; idiosyncrasy means per-model tooling is required.

**Direction:** For one safety concept, locate its representation (via probe or SAE feature) in three different open model families (e.g., Gemma, Llama, Qwen) and use representational-similarity / activation-correlation methods to test whether the feature plays an analogous causal role across them. Report a universality score for the concept.

**Why it matters:** Determines whether interpretability-based safety findings are portable across models — a key input to whether small-lab monitoring tools generalize. Pure inference on public weights, no training.

**Relevant context:** Feature universality is a recurring theme in mech interp (Olah et al.; '200 Concrete Open Problems'). Multi-model open weights (Gemma-2, Llama-3, Qwen3) and TransformerLens (50+ models) make cross-family activation comparison feasible.

# Attribution Graphs of a Refusal Decision in an Open Model

**Problem:** Circuit tracing has mostly been showcased on factual recall and poetry. The internal computation that produces a SAFETY refusal — and where exactly an effective jailbreak diverts that computation — has not been mapped with open attribution-graph tooling on a small open model.

**Direction:** Using the open Circuit Tracer library on a supported model (Gemma-2-2B / Qwen3-4B), build attribution graphs for a harmful request that is refused vs. the same request under a known jailbreak that succeeds. Identify which features/edges the jailbreak suppresses or reroutes to flip refusal to compliance.

**Why it matters:** Pinpointing the mechanistic 'pressure point' of refusal in an open model is directly useful for hardening safety and is reproducible outside any lab using released tooling — a concrete circuit-level safety contribution.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Circuit Tracing (transformer-circuits.pub 2025) introduced attribution graphs; open Circuit Tracer (Anthropic Fellows) supports Gemma-2-2B/Llama-3.2-1B/Qwen3-4B, EleutherAI's Attribute supports CLTs. Jailbreak datasets are public.

# Logit Lens as a Lightweight Sandbagging Tripwire

**Problem:** The logit lens reveals intermediate-layer token predictions, but it is rarely used as a safety monitor. If a model is sandbagging — internally 'knowing' a correct/capable answer it then suppresses — the logit lens might reveal the suppressed answer in mid-layers even when the final output underperforms.

**Direction:** Construct a small sandbagging setup on an open model (prompt it to underperform when it thinks it's evaluated) and apply the logit lens across layers to see whether the suppressed-but-known answer surfaces in intermediate layers. Test whether a simple mid-layer-vs-final divergence metric flags sandbagging.

**Why it matters:** A logit-lens tripwire would be an extremely cheap, training-free, infrastructure-free monitor for capability concealment — exactly the kind of lab-independent safety tooling prioritized here.

**Relevant context:** Logit lens is a standard mech-interp method (nostalgebraist; covered in Bereska review arXiv 2404.14082). Sandbagging is the most safety-critical deception type per deception-probe literature; near-zero compliance makes elicitation hard but small organism setups exist.

# Activation Patching to Localize a Hidden Goal in a Model Organism

**Problem:** A central long-horizon threat is a model pursuing a secret goal it never verbalizes in its chain-of-thought. There are public small 'model organism' setups with hidden objectives, but the localization of the hidden-goal representation (where in the network it lives, and whether it appears before any CoT) is under-studied with simple causal tools.

**Direction:** Take a publicly available hidden-goal model-organism prompt setup (or construct a minimal one via system-prompt injection of a secret objective) and use activation patching between goal-pursuing and neutral runs to localize the layers/positions carrying the hidden goal. Test whether the goal is represented before the CoT mentions anything.

**Why it matters:** Detecting hidden goals that bypass CoT monitoring is a core deceptive-alignment concern that labs deprioritize. Activation patching on a small open organism is feasible in 30h and needs zero proprietary access.

**Relevant context:** Activation patching / causal tracing are core methods (Bereska review arXiv 2404.14082). Model-organism studies of misalignment are an active open direction; CoT-bypassing hidden goals are a flagged long-horizon threat. TransformerLens supports patching.

# Multi-Hop Reasoning Circuits and Where They Silently Fail

**Problem:** Circuit tracing showed Claude forms intermediate representations in multi-hop questions (Dallas->Texas->Austin). When a model gets a multi-hop question WRONG, it is unknown whether the intermediate hop is absent, present-but-ignored, or corrupted — distinctions with different safety implications for reasoning reliability.

**Direction:** On an open model with the Circuit Tracer / logit-lens, take multi-hop questions the model answers correctly and incorrectly, and probe for the intermediate-entity representation in each case. Classify failures into 'missing intermediate', 'wrong intermediate', and 'correct intermediate but ignored'.

**Why it matters:** Understanding how internal reasoning fails (not just that it fails) is foundational for trusting model reasoning and for designing monitors. Reproducible on open models with released tooling.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic 'On the Biology of an LLM' (2025) reports multi-hop intermediate representations (Dallas->Texas->Austin). Open Circuit Tracer and logit-lens support intermediate-representation probing on small open models.

# Domain-Specific SAEs vs General SAEs for Niche Harm Detection

**Problem:** A 2025 result ('Resurrecting the Salmon') argues domain-specific SAEs can capture features general SAEs miss. For niche but high-stakes harm domains (e.g., bio/cyber-adjacent jargon), general SAEs may simply lack a clean feature, creating monitoring blind spots that nobody has measured.

**Direction:** Compare a general-corpus SAE against features extracted on a narrow domain corpus for whether a specific niche-harm concept gets a clean, monosemantic latent. Measure how much the general SAE 'misses' the concept versus a domain-focused feature search on the same model.

**Why it matters:** If general SAEs systematically miss niche harm concepts, monitoring built on them has predictable gaps in exactly the high-stakes long tail. This is diffuse, lab-independent evaluation work.

**Relevant context:** 'Resurrecting the Salmon: Rethinking Mech Interp with Domain-Specific SAEs' (arXiv 2508.09363) argues domain-specific SAEs capture features general SAEs miss. SAELens supports feature search; public domain corpora are available.

# Faithfulness of SAE Features Without External Dataset Dependence

**Problem:** FaithfulSAE argues that SAEs trained on external datasets can capture features that are artifacts of the dataset rather than the model, harming faithfulness. For safety monitoring this means a 'harm' feature might really track the audit dataset, not the model's own representation — a silent validity threat.

**Direction:** For one safety-relevant feature, compare a standard externally-trained SAE feature against a more model-faithful feature-extraction approach, and test whether the standard feature's activation is driven by dataset artifacts (e.g., surface tokens) versus genuine model-internal concept structure, using controlled minimal-pair prompts.

**Why it matters:** Validity of safety features is a precondition for any deployment decision built on them. Detecting dataset-artifact features needs only public models and small curated prompt sets — high counterfactual value.

**Relevant context:** 'FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features without External Dataset Dependencies' (arXiv 2506.17673) shows external-dataset SAEs capture dataset artifacts. SAE seed/hyperparameter instability (2025 reviews) compounds the validity concern.

# Cross-Lingual Stability of Safety Circuits in Open Models

**Problem:** Safety features and refusal circuits are almost always studied in English. Whether the same refusal/harm feature fires for semantically equivalent harmful prompts in other languages — or whether non-English inputs route around the safety circuit — is mechanistically under-explored on open multilingual models.

**Direction:** Locate a refusal/harm feature (probe or SAE) on an open multilingual model using English prompts, then test whether it activates for translated equivalents in 2-3 other languages. Quantify the activation gap and check whether successful multilingual jailbreaks correspond to feature non-activation.

**Why it matters:** Multilingual safety gaps are a real deployment risk and labs under-resource non-English safety. A mechanistic (not just behavioral) account is novel, lab-independent, and uses only open multilingual weights.

**Relevant context:** Multilingual open models (Gemma, Qwen, Aya) are public; TransformerLens/SAELens support activation extraction. Behavioral cross-lingual safety gaps are documented; the mechanistic feature-level account is the open angle here.

# Visual Concept Steering Side-Effects in CLIP via Prisma SAEs

**Problem:** Activation steering side-effects are documented for language models, but the analogous question for vision transformers — does steering a CLIP/ViT toward one visual concept cause collateral distortion of unrelated concepts — is unexplored, despite ViT-Prisma making the tools available.

**Direction:** Using ViT-Prisma pre-trained vision SAEs, pick a clean object/attribute feature, steer it during a forward pass, and measure both the intended effect (the target concept's classification) and collateral changes on a set of unrelated concepts. Map the vision-side steering side-effect profile.

**Why it matters:** As vision and multimodal models deploy in safety-critical settings, knowing whether interpretable interventions are surgical or messy on the vision side is important and entirely doable with public Prisma weights.

**Relevant context:** Joseph et al. 'Prisma' (arXiv 2504.19475) provides 80+ pre-trained vision SAE weights and steering tooling; vision SAEs have very high L0 (~500/patch). Language steering side-effects documented in 'The Rogue Scalpel' and 2025 steering reviews.

Release it with baseline scores for a few public SAE features so others can compare methods.

**Why it matters:** A shared yardstick is exactly the missing infrastructure flagged by Open Phil; even a small, well-specified prototype is strategically valuable and inherently lab-independent. The deliverable (benchmark + baselines + blog) is self-contained and valuable on its own.

**Relevant context:** Open Phil RFP and the subfield context flag the absence of interpretability benchmarks and the interpretability-to-safety-guarantee gap as priorities. Public SAEs (Neuronpedia/SAELens) and open models provide ready baseline material.

# Probe Robustness Under Decoding-Time Perturbations

**Problem:** Deception/refusal probes are evaluated on clean activations, but a model in deployment generates under varied sampling and with paraphrased inputs. Whether a monitoring probe's decision is stable when the same intent is expressed across paraphrases and decoding conditions is a robustness gap that undermines real monitoring.

**Direction:** Train a probe for one safety concept on an open model, then stress-test it against systematic paraphrases and benign distractor context injected around the same intent. Measure how much probe confidence drifts and identify the perturbation classes that most easily flip its decision.

**Why it matters:** A monitor that flips under trivial rephrasing gives false security. Characterizing this fragility is cheap, training-light, and directly informs whether probes are deployable — classic diffuse evaluation work.

**Relevant context:** 'Pressure-Testing Deception Probes' (arXiv 2605.27958) and probe-robustness literature show probes generalize poorly off-distribution. Open instruct models + simple paraphrase tooling make this a feasible 30h study.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic Circuit Tracing reports planning-ahead in Claude 3.5 Haiku; subfield hints explicitly suggest studying whether planning correlates with capability. Open model ladders (Pythia, Qwen3) and TransformerLens enable per-size analysis.

**Direction:** Using a small open multimodal model and Prisma/SAE tooling, take image+text prompts for one safety-relevant visual concept and trace at which layer the visual feature aligns with the corresponding language concept, testing whether refusal is driven by the visual feature or only by the later language-space feature.

**Relevant context:** 'How Visual Representations Map to Language Feature Space in Multimodal LLMs' (arXiv 2506.11976) and Prisma (arXiv 2504.19475) provide methods and weights. Extending mech interp to multimodal transformers is a listed open problem.
